When leadership does not own the culture, HR is left trying to enforce standards without authority or support. This is where accountability breaks down. Policies begin to feel optional. Expectations become inconsistent. And culture weakens. You can have the best strategy in the world, but it means very little if leaders refuse to model the culture they want to see in the organisation. People don’t follow policies, they follow behaviour. This is why I strongly advocate for HR to have a seat at Exco and be part of the senior management team. After years working on telecom and fibre-optic projects, one thing is clear: Delivery improves when uncertainty is acknowledged early, not hidden behind dashboards. Good PMs track work. Strong PMs reduce surprises. I’ve seen fibre rollouts stall not because tasks weren’t tracked, but because soil conditions changed, permits were delayed, or a supplier quietly missed a dependency. The dashboard was green, the risk wasn’t. On one telecom build, progress looked perfect until a late design assumption surfaced during field work. The PM who caught it early didn’t “push harder”, they reset scope, renegotiated timelines, and saved weeks of downstream rework. That’s the difference. Tools tell you where you are. This involves outlining tasks, timelines, and the resources needed to accomplish the project. Regular communication among team members is also vital; holding meetings to provide updates encourages collaboration and allows for the early identification of any issues. Additionally, assigning clear roles and responsibilities ensures that everyone knows their individual tasks, which helps streamline the workflow. Finally, monitoring progress and managing risks are key components of successful project management.
